questions.question_text:
A site plan is drawn to a scale of $1:300$.
A rectangular block on the plan measures $8$ cm by $5$ cm.
Find the real area of the block, in square metres.

options.why: Scaled the plan area by the linear factor, $40\times300=12\,000\text{ cm}^{2}$, instead of by $300^{2}$.
Scaled the area by $300^{2}$ correctly but left the answer in square centimetres instead of converting to square metres.
Found the real perimeter, $2(24+15)$, instead of the real area.

questions.question_text:
A plan of a warehouse is drawn to a scale of $1:150$.
On the plan the warehouse floor has an area of $24\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Find the real floor area, in square metres.

options.why: Scaled the area by the linear factor $150$ instead of by $150^{2}$, giving $3600\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Applied $150^{2}$ correctly but did not convert square centimetres to square metres.
Converted square centimetres to square metres by dividing by $100$ instead of by $10\,000$.

questions.question_text:
On a plan a rectangular tennis court measures $6$ cm by $3$ cm, and its real area is $648\text{ m}^{2}$.
Find the scale of the plan, in the form $1:n$.

options.why: Stopped at $n^{2}$ without taking the square root.
Divided the real area by the plan area in mixed units, $648\div18$, without converting square metres to square centimetres or taking a square root.
Took the square root of $648\div18$ but never converted the real area from square metres to square centimetres.

questions.question_text:
A survey plan is drawn to a scale of $1:2500$.
A triangular reserve has sides measuring $2.4$ cm, $3.2$ cm and $4$ cm on the plan.
Find the real perimeter of the reserve, in metres.

options.why: Added the three plan lengths and never applied the scale.
Applied the scale correctly but did not convert the centimetre total to metres.
Converted centimetres to metres by dividing by $10$ instead of by $100$.

questions.question_text:
A floor plan gives all measurements in millimetres.
A rectangular room measures $6300$ mm by $4200$ mm.
Find the perimeter of the room, in metres.

options.why: Multiplied the two side lengths, which gives the area, instead of adding right around the room.
Added the length and the width once only, forgetting that a rectangle has two of each.
Added right around the room in millimetres and did not convert the total to metres.

questions.question_text:
A floor plan gives all measurements in millimetres.
A rectangular garage measures $6000$ mm by $3600$ mm.
Find the floor area of the garage, in square metres.

options.why: Multiplied the two millimetre lengths and did not convert square millimetres to square metres.
Converted square millimetres to square metres by dividing by $1000$ instead of by $1\,000\,000$.
Found the perimeter of the garage instead of its area.

questions.question_text:
A map is drawn to a scale of $1:4000$.
A lake beside a straight road is measured with one application of the Trapezoidal rule: the strip width on the map is $4$ cm and the two end offsets are $1.5$ cm and $2.5$ cm.
Estimate the real surface area of the lake, in square metres.

options.why: Applied the rule to the map measurements and never used the scale at all.
Applied the rule to the map measurements and then scaled the resulting area by the linear factor $4000$ instead of scaling each length first.
Left out the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in $\dfrac{h}{2}$, multiplying the full strip width by the sum of the offsets.

questions.question_text:
An aerial photograph has a scale bar showing that $1$ cm represents $30$ m. A curved river frontage is surveyed from a straight baseline with offsets of $2$ cm, $3$ cm and $2.5$ cm, taken at equal intervals of $2$ cm along the photograph.
Use two applications of the Trapezoidal rule to estimate the real area, in square metres.

options.why: Used one application across the whole $120$ m width, ignoring the middle offset entirely.
Left out the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in $\dfrac{h}{2}$ in both applications.
Applied the rule to the photograph measurements and never used the scale bar.
